content.heading: 6.7 Inner Product Spaces
content.paragraph: Notions of length, distance, and orthogonality are often important in applications involving a vector space. For $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, these concepts were based on the properties of the inner product listed in Theorem 1 of Section 6.1. For other spaces, we need analogues of the inner product with the same properties. The conclusions of Theorem 1 now become axioms in the following definition.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: An inner product on a vector space $V$ is a function that, to each pair of vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $V$, associates a real number $\left\langle \mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\rangle$ and satisfies the following axioms, for all $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$, and $\textbf{w}$ in $V$ and all scalars $c$:

list.item: ⟨u, u⟩≥0 and ⟨u, u⟩=0 if and only if u=0

note.paragraph: A vector space with an inner product is called an inner product space .

content.paragraph: The vector space $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ with the standard inner product is an inner product space, and nearly everything discussed in this chapter for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ carries over to inner product spaces. The examples in this section and the next lay the foundation for a variety of applications treated in courses in engineering, physics, mathematics, and statistics.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Fix any two positive numbers—say, $4$ and $5$—and for vectors $\mathbf{u} = \left( u_{1}\text{,~}u_{2} \right)$ and $\mathbf{v} = \left( v_{1}\text{,~}v_{2} \right)$ in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, set
Show that equation (1) defines an inner product.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Certainly Axiom $1$ is satisfied, because $\left\langle \mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\rangle = 4u_{1}v_{1} + 5u_{2}v_{2} = {}4v_{1}u_{1} + 5v_{2}u_{2} = \left\langle \mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{u} \right\rangle$. If $\textbf{w} = \left( w_{1}\text{,~}w_{2} \right)$, then
This verifies Axiom $2$. For Axiom $3$, compute

For Axiom $4$, note that $\left\langle \mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{u} \right\rangle = 4u_{1}^{2} + 5u_{2}^{2} \geq 0$, and $4u_{1}^{2} + 5u_{2}^{2} = 0$ only if $u_{1} = u_{2} = 0$, that is, if $\mathbf{u} = \textbf{0}$. Also, $\left\langle \textbf{0}\text{,~}\textbf{0} \right\rangle = 0$. So (1) defines an inner product on $\text{ℝ}^{2}$.

content.paragraph: Inner products similar to (1) can be defined on $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. They arise naturally in connection with “weighted least-squares” problems, in which weights are assigned to the various entries in the sum for the inner product in such a way that more importance is given to the more reliable measurements.

From now on, when an inner product space involves polynomials or other functions, we will write the functions in the familiar way, rather than use the boldface type for vectors. Nevertheless, it is important to remember that each function is a vector when it is treated as an element of a vector space.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $t_{0}$, $\ldots$, $t_{n}$ be distinct real numbers. For $p$ and $q$ in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$, define

paragraph.math: $$\left\langle p\text{,~}q \right\rangle = p\left( t_{0} \right)q\left( t_{0} \right) + p\left( t_{1} \right)q\left( t_{1} \right) + \cdots + p\left( t_{n} \right)q\left( t_{n} \right)$$

example.paragraph: Inner product Axioms $1–3$ are readily checked. For Axiom $4$, note that

paragraph.math: $$\left\langle p\text{,~}p \right\rangle = \lbrack p\left( t_{0} \right)\rbrack^{2} + \lbrack p\left( t_{1} \right)\rbrack^{2} + \cdots + \lbrack p\left( t_{n} \right)\rbrack^{2} \geq 0$$

example.paragraph: Also, $\left\langle \textbf{0}\text{,~}\textbf{0} \right\rangle = 0$. (The boldface zero here denotes the zero polynomial, the zero vector in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$.) If $\left\langle p\text{,~}p \right\rangle = 0$, then $p$ must vanish at $n + 1$ points: $t_{0}$, $\ldots$, $t_{n}$. This is possible only if $p$ is the zero polynomial, because the degree of $p$ is less than $n + 1$. Thus (2) defines an inner product on $\text{ℙ}_{n}$.

content.heading: Lengths, Distances, and Orthogonality
content.paragraph: Let $V$ be an inner product space, with the inner product denoted by $\left\langle \mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\rangle$. Just as in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, we define the length, or norm, of a vector $\mathbf{v}$ to be the scalar

Equivalently, $\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2} = \left\langle \mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\rangle$. (This definition makes sense because $\left\langle \mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\rangle \geq 0$, but the definition does not say that $\left\langle \mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\rangle$ is a “sum of squares,” because $\mathbf{v}$ need not be an element of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.)

A unit vector is one whose length is $1$. The distance between ﻿u and v is $\parallel \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$. Vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are orthogonal if $\left\langle \mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\rangle = 0$.

content.heading: The Gram–Schmidt Process
content.paragraph: The existence of orthogonal bases for finite-dimensional subspaces of an inner product space can be established by the Gram–Schmidt process, just as in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Certain orthogonal bases that arise frequently in applications can be constructed by this process.

The orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace $W$ with an orthogonal basis can be constructed as usual. The projection does not depend on the choice of orthogonal basis, and it has the properties described in the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem and the Best Approximation Theorem.

content.heading: Best Approximation in Inner Product Spaces
content.paragraph: A common problem in applied mathematics involves a vector space $V$ whose elements are functions. The problem is to approximate a function $f$ in $V$ by a function $g$ from a specified subspace $W$ of $V$. The “closeness” of the approximation of $f$ depends on the way $\parallel f - g \parallel$ is defined. We will consider only the case in which the distance between $f$ and $g$ is determined by an inner product. In this case, the best approximation to$f$by functions in$W$is the orthogonal projection of $f$ onto the subspace $W$.

content.heading: An Inner Product for C[a, b] (Calculus required)
content.paragraph: Probably the most widely used inner product space for applications is the vector space $C\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$ of all continuous functions on an interval $a \leq t \leq b$, with an inner product that we will describe.

We begin by considering a polynomial $p$ and any integer $n$ larger than or equal to the degree of $p$. Then $p$ is in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$, and we may compute a “length” for $p$ using the inner product of Example 2 involving evaluation at $n + 1$ points in $\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$. However, this length of $p$ captures the behavior at only those $n + 1$ points. Since $p$ is in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ for all large $n$, we could use a much larger $n$, with many more points for the “evaluation” inner product. See Figure 4.

figure.label: Figure 4
figure.caption: Using different numbers of evaluation points in [a, b] to compute ∥p∥2

image.alt: Two curves labeled p (t) are plotted above a horizontal axis.

content.paragraph: Let us partition $\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$ into $n + 1$ subintervals of length $\text{Δ}t = (b - a)/(n + 1)$, and let $t_{0}$, $\ldots$, $t_{n}$ be arbitrary points in these subintervals.

image.alt: A figure shows a straight line with three subintervals.

content.paragraph: If $n$ is large, the inner product on $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ determined by $t_{0}$, $\ldots$, $t_{n}$ will tend to give a large value to $\left\langle p\text{,~}p \right\rangle$, so we scale it down and divide by $n + 1$. Observe that $1/(n + 1) = \text{Δ}t/(b - a)$, and define

Now, let $n$ increase without bound. Since polynomials $p$ and $q$ are continuous functions, the expression in brackets is a Riemann sum that approaches a definite integral, and we are led to consider the average value of$p(t)q(t)$ on the interval $\left\lbrack a\text{,~}b \right\rbrack$:

This quantity is defined for polynomials of any degree (in fact, for all continuous functions), and it has all the properties of an inner product, as the next example shows. The scale factor $1/(b - a)$ is inessential and is often omitted for simplicity.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: For $f$, $g$ in $C\left\lbrack a\text{,~}b \right\rbrack$, set
Show that (5) defines an inner product on $C\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Inner product Axioms $\text{1–3}$ follow from elementary properties of definite integrals. For Axiom $4$, observe that

The function $\left\lbrack {f(t)} \right\rbrack^{2}$ is continuous and nonnegative on $\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$. If the definite integral of $\left\lbrack {f(t)} \right\rbrack^{2}$ is zero, then $\left\lbrack {f(t)} \right\rbrack^{2}$ must be identically zero on $\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$, by a theorem in advanced calculus, in which case $f$ is the zero function. Thus $\left\langle f\text{,~}f \right\rangle = 0$ implies that $f$ is the zero function on $\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$. So (5) defines an inner product on $C\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$.
